title: Guitar Theory
intro: Guitar theory is ordinary music theory, the same intervals, scales and chords as on the piano, seen through the fretboard. The guitar's grid of strings and frets makes every pattern movable, but also lets one pitch appear in up to five places. These pages take the piano-based Music Theory topic as their reference and focus on what is particular to the guitar.

blocks.text: On a piano each pitch has exactly one key and the layout is a line. On the guitar the same pitch can be played on several strings, and the neck is a grid: one fret along a string is a semitone, one string across is (usually) a fourth. That gives the guitar its central advantage: a shape is movable. A chord or scale pattern played at one fret becomes the same chord or scale in another key by sliding it up or down. The piano needs different fingerings in different keys; the guitar mostly does not.

The cost is that guitarists can play without knowing the note names, using shapes alone. These pages connect the two: each shape is explained by the intervals in it, so the theory terms (major third, dominant seventh, Dorian) mean the same thing here as in Music Theory (#/arts/music-theory/).

items: The two irregularities to remember: strings are a fourth apart except G–B (a major third), and the fretboard repeats every 12 frets.
Everything a semitone apart on the piano is one fret apart on a string.
Moving a shape across from the G string onto the B string means moving it up one fret to compensate for the major third.
The Fretboard (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/fretboard): finding every note, octave shapes and the repeating 12-fret pattern.
Intervals as Shapes (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/intervals-and-shapes): every interval as a fixed fingering, and the G–B shift.
Scales on the Guitar (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/scales): major-scale patterns, the five pentatonic boxes, modes on the neck.
The CAGED System (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/caged): five open-chord shapes that map the whole neck.
Chord Voicings (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/chord-voicings): open and barre chords, power chords, triads on string sets, drop-2 and shell voicings.
Harmony and Progressions (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/harmony-and-progressions): diatonic chords up the neck, the Nashville number system, the capo and common progressions.
Soloing over Chords (#/arts/guitar/guitar-theory/soloing): target notes, arpeggios and the blues.

blocks.text: Sources: Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press; Tagliarino, B. (2006). Guitar Fretboard Workbook. Hal Leonard; Levine, M. (1995). The Jazz Theory Book. Sher Music.
